result.delta_one_sentence: A takes the estimator that B's workflow only describes (record routing traces, replay them through cache policies, turn misses into tokens/s) and makes it a falsifiable predictor: a three-tier time model (engine cache, OS file cache, SSD) that uses the target engine's exact eviction rule, fits one constant, and is tested against 11 independent held-out speeds, within-run contrasts and a frozen baseline; B instead offers a working streaming engine and direct single-prompt measurements of the 1T model, with an estimator that is unvalidated and calibrated on its own runs.
result.reasoning:
Same mechanism: yes, for the estimation part. Both record which experts are selected at each layer, replay those selections through per-layer cache policies (LRU, static or pinned sets) and convert the misses into decode speed for SSD streaming of a 384-expert, top-8, 1T MoE on a 128 GB laptop. B's companion workflow prescribes almost exactly A's pipeline. B's engine itself (a side file of extracted experts, a slot bank with LRU refill, temporal prefetch) is a systems contribution that A does not attempt. A builds no engine.

Why A is the stronger research contribution:
(1) Validation. A tests its model on 11 published speeds that were not used to build it, on two other models. It also uses within-run contrasts with identical routing, so the shared calibration error cancels, and it must beat a frozen baseline that derives hit rates from cache size alone. B's estimator is calibrated on anchors from the same engine (baseline, banked, oracle all-hit), publishes no outputs and is never checked against held-out conditions. It is a recipe, not a result.
(2) Model fidelity. A models the OS file cache as a separate tier, bounded by the free memory logged for each run, and also models cold starts and both prefill paths. B's own data suggests this tier matters. At four experts, decode stays flat at 3.2-3.3 tok/s while per-call hit rate rises from 55.6% to 76.4%. So in B's runs the bank misses barely limit speed: something cheaper, plausibly the file cache, or a fixed overhead dominates. A simple LRU-misses-to-SSD conversion like B's would mispredict this.
(3) Workload realism. A traces four session types, includes 8K-16K-token documents and up to 2,048 tokens per session, and chooses the frequency-pinned set on held-out sessions. B has one greedy prompt and 100 tokens from a cold start, mostly with routing halved to four experts. Its hit rates are therefore biased by warm-up and do not reflect native routing.

B's real advantages:
- B has ground truth that A deliberately lacks. It measured the 1T model on the target laptop: 2.2 tok/s at native top-8 with 64 slots, a 67.2% hit rate and about 4.7 GB/s reads.
- B ships a usable engine with a trace format.

A's risks:
- Its 1T prediction extrapolates from smaller validation models into a regime where the cache covers a much smaller share of the experts and the SSD dominates.
- Its single constant comes from one measurement.
- Its 11 anchors come from published runs whose conditions it does not control.
- It should use B's measured numbers as an extra out-of-sample check, even though B uses a different engine and a different quantisation.

On balance A is the more rigorous and more novel contribution: a validated, decision-grade predictor rather than an engine with anecdotal benchmarks and an untested estimation recipe.

Feasibility.lens: Feasibility: is the pilot decisive, can it run on this host within 8 GPU-h before 2026-10-21 with the assets available, and is the full study affordable and able to change a decision
Feasibility.strongest_argument:
The pilot can probably run on the host, but it is not decisive. The one decision it outputs is wired to the wrong program lines, and the reading it is most likely to give can already be forecast from the bundle's own numbers.

(1) The decision rule closes lines that a streaming ratio cannot close. Proposal section 7.1 says G1, G3 and G5's "only Mac rationale is a Kimi that streams competitively". The dossier says otherwise:
- G1 and G3 are about a Kimi of 100-105 GB or less that sits in memory. Dossier K6 says "held in memory: 18-24 tok/s", and G1 says to use "A4 for files that fit in memory, the G2 emulator otherwise". A ratio R between streamed Kimi K2.6 Q2 and streamed GLM 5.3 therefore says nothing about G1 or G3.
- G5 exists to make streamed Kimi faster: top-6 is 28-30% faster and top-4 76-87% faster at a fixed hit rate (dossier section 3e and G5). A top-8 R below 1 is exactly the case that motivates G5. Yet the rule closes G5 under KIMI_DOMINATED, and it runs F5 (the top-6 and top-4 traces) only under KIMI_COMPETITIVE. That is backwards.

(2) The likely outcome is already known. These figures come from the bundle's `identification-g2stream.json` and `ds4-targets.json`, with B at about 6 GB/s:
- With all other work stopped, the dossier null predicts 2.5-3.6 tok/s for Kimi. ds4 measured GLM 5.3 at 5.11-5.39 tok/s at 61 GiB. Kimi needs h of at least about 0.86 at 22.7% of its pool just to tie, and R's upper bound must stay below 1 in both scenarios for KIMI_DOMINATED.
- At today's free memory the null predicts 1.45-1.75 tok/s for Kimi, against GLM measured at 3.66-3.89 at 35 GiB.
- So, given that R gets computed at all, KIMI_DOMINATED is about 85-90% likely. That reading already matches the desk default: GLM 45 against Kimi 27 on the C32 index, and the kill-shot cell's own concession that "no G2 outcome alone makes streamed Kimi the right default".

(3) The chance that R gets computed at all is modest:
- Even an unbiased emulator passes the three contrasts only 79% of the time by the proposal's own Monte Carlo, and 22-37% with a 10% mechanism bias.
- K2 and K3 rest on CANDIDATE-fidelity inputs, because the appended tokens are unpublished.
- If the P1-gpu fallback runs, the 32 GLM matched sessions are dropped by design, so R is not computed and the reading is UNRESOLVED.
- If validation fails (LEVELS_ONLY or FAILED), the reading is EMULATOR_NOT_TRUSTED and the dossier keeps its brackets.

(4) R prices an engine that does not exist. ds4 does not run Kimi, and D122 records that no maintained Mac streamer supports Kimi. The registration itself says it "does not decide what Kevin should run on his Mac".

Bottom line: the full study (15-41 GPU-h) is affordable. But its trigger (KIMI_COMPETITIVE or UNRESOLVED on top-8 R) still does not bear on G1 or G3, and it holds back G5's input in the UNRESOLVED case. No branch correctly changes a program decision.
Feasibility.what_would_change_my_mind:
Two changes to the decision rule would make the pilot decisive:
- Fix the wiring. Gate only on lines that actually depend on streamed speed (G5, and any streamed version of G1 above 128 GB). Drop G1 and G3, which are in memory. Make the top-4 and top-6 R (from replaying the traces at reduced top-k, or a small F5 slice inside the pilot) the statistic that decides G5, with closure only if the top-4 R also stays below 1.
- Commit, before data, a desk prior for R, and show it has a real chance of exceeding 1, for example h of 0.86 or more at 22.7% being plausible from the K2-family evidence (Anemll's 67% at 16.7% per-layer, S82's K3 LRU 44%).

On feasibility, two things would remove the run-time risk:
- A measured P2 throughput showing the run fits in 1.0 h with both reloads and with 2,048-token thinking sessions, or a P2 limit raised within the 8 GPU-h line.
- A measured CPU-lane GLM prefill rate showing the 32 matched sessions finish inside 12 h.

Identification.lens: Identification: the predicted effect is confounded, leaks, or is not caused by the mechanism (routing locality plus cache policy). Checked for GGUF-versus-INT4 routing, workload choice, ds4 single-run noise, unknown SSD, the included first-token wait, and whether the outcomes measure what they claim.
Identification.strongest_argument:
The pilot rests on one identifying assumption, and ds4's own numbers contradict it. The assumption is that CAL-B, the 30.8 s whole-layer 16-token append, is a prompt-independent full read of the 186.86 GB routed pool. That would pin B at 6.08 GB/s and break the h/B degeneracy.

1. **CAL-B is not a pure SSD rate.** The same 61.35 GiB runs did a 1,024-token initial prefill at 55.92 and 55.16 t/s, about 18.3 s (QA_BEFORE_RELEASES.md at 90aa4b56). Registration section 8.1 says initial prefill reads every routed layer's whole tensors per chunk, and the chunk is at least 1,024. So that prefill is also a full 186.86 GB read.
   - At B = 6.08 the emulator predicts 29.5 t/s for it, about 1.9 times too slow.
   - Even if all 15.05 GiB of file cache were hits and compute were zero, the run implies at least 9.3 GB/s. A third-party measurement of the M5 Max reads 13.6 GB/s sustained.
   - So B absorbs at least 12 s of whole-layer-path overhead, or file-cache dynamics the registration fixes at the logged minimum. This row appears nowhere in ds4-targets.json: not as a holdout, not as secondary, not as excluded.
   - The null under-predicting 10 of 11 rows at B = 6.08 (M2) is then explained just as well by a mis-identified B as by the file-cache tier.
2. **The primary contrasts do not isolate locality.**
   - K2 has identical routing in both arms. Its gap is 64/4.09 − 64/5.11 = 3.12 s.
   - ds4 documents a page-in of non-routed weights after a prompt, and the proposal's own C26 (rustane) documents page-cache eviction of backbone weights. At the proposal's own B, GLM's 19.72 GB of non-routed bytes takes 3.24 s, within 4% of the gap.
   - The registration applies τ_first uniformly "after every prefill", with a central value of 0. It therefore cannot represent a path-dependent first-token cost. A K2 or PR3 pass would credit the file-cache or expert-cache state for an effect the engine's own documentation attributes to the backbone page-in.
   - ds4-bench records first-token time separately (gen_first_ms), but ds4 publishes only rates that include it. The two mechanisms cannot be separated from the targets.
   - V5i (3.78) and V5bi (4.14) have identical routing. Using V5bi instead of V5i moves K3 from 1.352 to 1.234, which is 65% of the ±15% band.
3. **Even a VALIDATED verdict cannot license the decision.**
   - ds4 runs only DeepSeek V4 and GLM 5.x. R's numerator is Kimi on an engine that does not exist, and registration section 2 says the verdict "says nothing about engines other than ds4".
   - CONTRASTS_ONLY still reports R. But a cross-model ratio does not cancel B or e: R goes from 0.80 to 0.92 as B goes from 6.08 to 13.6 GB/s, and the B bracket only goes down (0.5×).
   - KIMI_DOMINATED closes G1, which is an in-memory Kimi of about 100 GB, not a streamed one. It also closes G5, whose rationale is that top-4 streams 76-87% faster. A top-8 streamed R measures neither.
4. **The locality estimand is inflated by the decoding choice.** All 64 primary Kimi sessions use greedy decoding with thinking on, against the model card's temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.95. Greedy decoding with thinking is known to cause repetition loops, which push h up, as the apple prompt shows. The Kimi decode cap is also 2,048 tokens against 1,024 for the matched GLM sessions, which biases R upward.

Novelty.lens: Novelty: is the measurement (Kimi K2.x expert-cache hit-rate curves) or the emulator (a three-tier Mac streaming time model validated against held-out ds4 M5 Max results) already published, or is it a trivial recombination?
Novelty.strongest_argument:
I found no direct prior for either half. Nothing published gives K2.x hit-rate curves on long-decode chat, agentic or long-document sessions, and nothing validates a streaming emulator against held-out Mac measurements. The emulator is still a recombination of published parts, and the proposal misses the strongest of them.

The novelty ledger rests the emulator's delta on three things: the file-cache tier (the engine reads without F_NOCACHE, so the macOS file cache serves misses), the held-out discipline, and the K2 workload curves. The file-cache tier is not new. Six public sources describe the same mechanism and the same symptom (hit rate rises while tokens per second falls on unified-memory Apple Silicon):
- danveloper/flash-moe (2026-03): "Trust the OS"; deleting the Metal LRU gave +38%; the page cache reaches about 71% hits.
- rustane (C26).
- MawForge (arXiv 2607.09686, 2026-06-17), a 600-row M5 Pro matrix: "hit rate and throughput diverge".
- kk-r/dsv4-streaming (2026-08-15): hit rate 0.434 to 0.669 while speed falls 2.04 to 1.23 tok/s, explained as the app cache evicting the page cache because files are opened without F_NOCACHE.
- ds4 issue #810 (same author, same day, on ds4 itself): an 8 GB cache beats 32 GB on an M5 Pro.
- S82's Darwin replay.

The proposal cites only rustane and S82 for this. The dossier lists flash-moe (S50/S135), MawForge (S88) and Colibri (S52), but the proposal never credits them against the file-cache delta.

The trace, policy simulation and held-out pipeline is also published:
- Colibri's CNRE offline residency simulator (docs/experiments/cnre-offline-simulator.md, 2026-08-08 to 2026-09-20) replays ROUTE_TRACE through LRU, decayed LFU, segmented LRU and pinned+LRU caches, with trace-trained residents scored on held-out categories (chat, code, reasoning, multilingual, long-context). It has a per-layer miss-cost model (read GB/s × felt fraction) calibrated from PROF logs, and sensitivity bands. Its H200 runtime pilot found 73.5% hits at 1.31 tok/s against 57.2% at 1.66.
- Anemll's published flashmoe_cache_estimator.py already runs per-layer static, global static and LRU simulation on Kimi --moe-trace JSONL. The bank-modeling workflow adds the calibration to runtime anchors.

The K2 curves are a textbook cache simulation applied to a new model. Released K2-Thinking per-token, per-layer traces exist (Chaos; 31,593 files), and Anemll's estimator plus its K2.5 measurement (67.2% at 64 slots) exist too. What differs is the checkpoint (K2.6 Q2), decode length (up to 2,048 tokens) and workload mix. Those are parameter changes, not a new mechanism.

What survives is narrow:
- K2.6-specific numbers on four workloads;
- the act of testing an assembled model against ds4's published rows, including the within-run contrasts.

That is a validation exercise over known components, not a new emulator or measurement method. The proposal itself already names this recombination risk. Given the default-to-refuted rule, I count this as refuted on the trivial-recombination prong.
Novelty.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any of these would move me to not-refuted:
- The proposal drops the file-cache tier as a novelty delta, credits flash-moe, MawForge, kk-r/dsv4-streaming, ds4 #810 and Colibri CNRE, and states the claimed contribution as (a) K2.6 measurement data and (b) a pre-registered held-out validation test, not a new emulator.
- A blind critic reliably tells the proposal apart from a fused paragraph of Anemll + Colibri CNRE + kk-r, specifically on the within-run-contrast validation design (identical-routing pairs in which the calibration error cancels). No source I found does that.
- Evidence that the emulator needs a non-obvious modelling element absent from all priors (for example, an identification of ds4's file-cache capacity from its logged available memory that changes predictions measurably beyond a bytes/bandwidth + hit rate + page-cache model).

Conversely, any public result would make the refutation decisive:
- LRU or decayed-hotness hit rates computed on the Chaos K2 traces;
- K2.5 or K2.6 traces from the Anemll fork or Colibri;
- a tok/s predictor for ds4 or Colibri checked against measured runs.

synthesis_result.mechanism_paragraph: A study asks how well the expert-cache behaviour of a one-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model (384 routed experts per layer, eight selected per token plus one shared expert, 60 routed layers) can be predicted for SSD streaming on a 128 GB unified-memory laptop without running anything on the laptop. On a server it records which experts are selected for every token and layer. The routing comes from the about-2.6-bit file a laptop would stream, generating its own responses in four kinds of session: chat, coding, multi-turn tool use replayed from recorded trajectories, and question answering over 8K-16K-token documents, with up to 2,048 decoded tokens each. It replays these selections event by event, so that one token's eight experts at one layer form one cache event, through several policies: least-recently-used, least-frequently-used, a frequency-pinned set chosen on held-out sessions, an offline optimum, and the exact eviction policy of a published laptop streaming engine (per-expert selection counts halved every 16 decoded tokens, lowest count evicted, ties broken by recency). It feeds the per-layer misses into a time model with three storage tiers, because that engine reads experts with ordinary buffered file reads: the engine's own expert cache, the operating system's file cache (capacity bounded by the free memory logged for each published run) and the SSD. The model includes cold starts and the engine's two prefill paths, whole-layer reads and selected-expert reads. Exactly one constant is fitted: the SSD read rate, taken from a single published measurement whose cost does not depend on the prompt, a short append that read the whole expert pool. Everything else is fixed in advance. The model is then tested against eleven held-out published decode speeds of two other models on the target laptop. It is also tested on three within-run contrasts that change only cache state or the code path, with identical routing, so the shared calibration error cancels. It must beat a frozen baseline that derives hit rates from cache size alone. Only if it passes does the study predict the large model's laptop decode speed, as a ratio to an already-measured model on the same sessions, and use that ratio to decide whether compressing the large model for laptop use is worth pursuing.
